analysis.one_liner: Lets corporations deduct the dividends they pay from their taxable income.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors and never left the Ways and Means Committee, dying when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change corporate tax rules so that a domestic corporation can deduct the dividends it pays to shareholders, the same way it deducts interest on debt. That would wipe out the corporate-level tax on profits paid out to stockholders. To cover part of the cost, it repeals the deductions corporations currently get for dividends they receive, ends special tax treatment of public utility preferred stock, and raises the deduction for dividends from partly owned foreign corporations from 80% to 85%.
analysis.who_benefits: Shareholders of dividend-paying corporations, especially the large and wealthy stockholders who own most corporate shares. A corporation paying $100 million in dividends would deduct that $100 million, cutting its tax bill by up to the corporate rate on that amount.

how_it_helps.text: Allows every domestic corporation (except S corporations, mutual funds, REITs, and personal holding companies) a deduction equal to the dividends it pays during the year [S3].

Reduces the double taxation of corporate earnings: profits are taxed once at the corporate level and again when distributed as dividends; the deduction removes the second layer at the corporate level [S2].
Raises from 80% to 85% the deduction corporations may claim for dividends received from a 10%-owned foreign corporation [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury and, through lost federal revenue, ordinary taxpayers generally. The bill also raises taxes on corporations holding public utility preferred stock by repealing those dividends-received and dividends-paid deductions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; some utilities and their stockholders

drawbacks.text: The dividends-paid deduction would be a large revenue loss to the Treasury, borne by all taxpayers, and the benefit flows mainly to corporate shareholders, who are disproportionately high-income [S3].

The offsetting repeals hit other taxpayers: corporations lose deductions for dividends they receive, and the repeal of sections 244 and 247 ends long-standing deductions tied to public utility preferred stock [S2] [S3].

Because dividends become deductible while interest on debt already is, the tax code would treat debt and equity nearly alike at the corporate level — but only for dividends paid out, so the change is partial and its effect on corporate financing choices is untested.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Ending the double taxation of distributed profits is a real, defensible policy goal, and the bill pairs the new deduction with offsetting repeals rather than adding purely to the deficit. But the balance still favors stockholders: the dividends-paid deduction is far larger than the repealed deductions, the gain concentrates among wealthier households that own the most stock, and the utility preferred-stock repeals raise costs on a financing channel ordinary retail investors and ratepayers have historically used. It is a targeted tax cut dressed as a reform.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on the first day of the 104th Congress and referred to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Dornan introduced the bill on January 4, 1995, the opening day of the 104th Congress [S1] [S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S5].
No cosponsors ever signed on [S4], and the action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor action after the referral [S5].
The bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody gained directly, because nothing happened. Federal taxpayers kept the existing rules, which continue to collect tax on dividends at the corporate level, while dividend-paying corporations never received the deduction.

for.name: Rep. Robert K. Dornan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors joined from either party, so no partisan split is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill lets corporations deduct dividends paid, cutting their tax bills in proportion to payouts; since corporate shares are held disproportionately by wealthier households, the tax savings concentrate at the top while the revenue cost spreads across all taxpayers.

The bill repeals the special deductions for dividends on utility preferred stock (paid and received), raising taxes on that traditional financing channel, but utilities paying common dividends would gain the new general dividends-paid deduction.

industries.industry: U.S. corporations with stakes in foreign affiliates
industries.note: The deduction for dividends received from a 10%-owned foreign corporation rises from 80% to 85%, cutting tax on income flowing back from abroad.
